transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-12-21 15:00 UTC, duration ~52m
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Jordan Lee (Redwood SE), Alex Rivera (CTO - Paladin), Priya Patel (Lead ML Eng - Paladin), Sanjeev Rao (Head of Infra - Paladin)

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time, uh this is Maya from Redwood, i'm joined by Jordan, our SE who's been deep in embeddings and reranking - thanks for joining.
[00:18] Alex Rivera: Thanks Maya, yeah appreciate it. Quick context — we run a security knowledge base + alerts product, and we're looking to improve search quality for triage and investigator workflows. Currently elasticsearch and some homegrown re-ranker.
[00:35] Priya Patel: Yeah most of our queries are short, like 1-3 tokens sometimes more, and we need both recall for discovery and reranking for precision. We're exploring embeddings + rerank approach.
[00:48] Jordan Lee: cool, so typical pattern we see is lexical retrieval (ES / BM25) for recall, then embed-based reranking for semantic precision. We support both hosted embedding endpoints and dedicated infra if you need predictable throughput.
[01:05] Priya Patel: Can Redwood hook up directly to our existing ES cluster or do we have to move data to Pinecone or milvus?
[01:12] Jordan Lee: good question — you don't have to move data. Common approaches: 1) keep ES as the primary index and store embeddings alongside docs in ES, 2) push only embeddings to a vector DB like Pinecone/Weaviate/FAISS for fast ANN, or 3) hybrid — ES for lexical then call Redwood to fetch embeddings and rerank. We have connectors and patterns for all three.
[01:36] Alex Rivera: Are connectors first-class? We want minimal engineering churn.
[01:40] Maya Chen: connectors are patterns, not a black box; our SEs will provide starter scripts. Jordan, maybe share typical latency numbers?
[01:46] Jordan Lee: sure. For a hosted Redwood embeddings + rerank flow — if you do ES top-K 100 and then call rerank on top 50, expect end-to-end p95 around 220-450ms depending on model size and batching. If you need sub-100ms we'd recommend dedicated reserved pools with tuned batching and caching. Oh and full disclosure, those numbers depend on dims and model family, quantization, and sequence lengths.
[02:12] Priya Patel: dims — we currently use 512 for some models, 1536 for others. What's your guidance on dimensionality tradeoffs?
[02:20] Jordan Lee: Generally larger dims like 1536 give better semantic separability for complex documents but cost more in memory and ANN latency. For short QA and throughput-sensitive systems, 512 is a common sweet spot. We can evaluate loss in accuracy vs unit-cost in the PoC. Also we support mixed precision / quantization profiles to reduce memory.
[02:39] Sanjeev Rao: We have throughput targets — peak 800 qps to the search service, with 100 qps dedicated to reranking in spikes. Can Redwood Dedicated handle that?
[02:49] Jordan Lee: yes, Dedicated reserved GPU pools are for that predictability. You can configure autoscaling and burst capacity. For 100 qps rerank at, say, 512-dim re-ranker with optimized kernels, we've seen setups handle that with steady p95 under 200ms. We'll need details about top-K, vector size, and batch window to size precisely.
[03:12] Alex Rivera: How does hybrid search work with Elasticsearch? We don't want double calls or high egress.
[03:20] Jordan Lee: typical pattern: ES returns top-N lexical candidates, then you fetch embeddings for those doc ids (either from ES if stored or from vector DB), call Redwood rerank API which does similarity and final scoring. You can run embeddings locally on Redwood Private or fetch embeddings via a stored vector DB. We also have an approach where you persist cached embeddings in Redis or local KV so reranks don't require recompute. Note — egress can be minimized by colocating vector DB in same region or using Private deployment to avoid public egress.
[03:54] Priya Patel: Security: we need SOC2 within our vendor stack and KMS integration for key management. Also SSO with SAML.
[04:03] Maya Chen: Redwood is SOC 2 type 2 and we have ISO27001 docs; we support customer-managed KMS for Private deployments and bring-your-own-key for Dedicated. SSO/SAML and RBAC are supported in Console. We'll send the security pack after this call.
[04:20] Sanjeev Rao: For private deployment — we need VPC peering and no public internet access for data. Is on-prem an option?
[04:28] Jordan Lee: yes, Private mode supports VPC-only control planes and an on-prem package for air-gapped. There are different operational models; we'll map your constraints and propose a network diagram.
[04:40] Alex Rivera: What about vector DB vendors? We're evaluating Pinecone and Weaviate; also looked at running FAISS ourselves. Pros/cons?
[04:48] Jordan Lee: quick take: Pinecone is fully managed and low friction; Weaviate offers schema and plugin ecosystem (and vector-indexed metadata); self-hosted FAISS is flexible but operationally heavy. Redwood can integrate with any — for high throughput we often recommend colocated vector indexes in same cloud region and use dedicated pools for low latency.
[05:12] Priya Patel: If we pick 1536-dim embeddings, how much memory are we looking at for say 10M docs?
[05:19] Jordan Lee: approximate math: 1536 dims * 4 bytes = ~6KB per vector, so 10M ~60GB raw, but ANN indexes add overhead — you'd be looking at 2x-4x depending on index type, so plan for a few hundred GB. Quantization can cut that by 4x-8x. We'll include sizing guidelines in the PoC plan.
[05:42] Priya Patel: Our latency SLO for rerank is 150ms p95 for investigator UI; we may accept 300ms for batch analytics. Is that realistic?
[05:52] Jordan Lee: 150ms p95 is achievable with Dedicated and caching, plus top-K tuning (smaller K), and prefix caching for repeated queries. Hosted can sometimes meet it but depends on tenancy; Dedicated is safer.
[06:08] Alex Rivera: Cost — what's the main cost driver?
[06:12] Maya Chen: the drivers are model family (bigger models cost more compute), tokens for generation flows, and persistent infrastructure for vector indexes (memory / storage). For rerank-only workloads, per-request compute and vector DB costs dominate. Our Optimize tooling can recommend batching / quantization to reduce unit cost. We'll send an example unit economics sheet.
[06:30] Priya Patel: Benchmarks — we'd like Redwood to run a rerank benchmark on a sample of our queries with our scoring metric.
[06:36] Jordan Lee: absolutely. Typical PoC structure: you provide sample dataset and target label set, we run comparisons between embedding dims and model variants, measure recall@k, MRR, and latency/cost. We'll propose a two-week PoC.
[06:50] Sanjeev Rao: Network egress — if we go Hosted, do we pay egress for pulling vector payloads?
[06:55] Maya Chen: egress depends on where your vector DB sits. If your ES/vector DB is in your cloud and you call Redwood Hosted across the internet, egress charges may apply. Private deployment can avoid that. We'll include network options in the architecture doc.
[07:12] Alex Rivera: Any quick wins to try before a PoC?
[07:16] Jordan Lee: you could start by storing 512-dim embeddings for critical docs, try lexical + embedding rerank with a small top-K, and measure improvement — often gives immediate UX lift. Also lower dims + quantization typically keeps most signal at much lower cost.
[07:33] Priya Patel: Are there SDKs or repos for the ES + rerank pattern?
[07:37] Maya Chen: yes, we'll share our quickstart repo that shows ES + Redwood rerank with example scripts and sample Docker compose.
[07:45] Alex Rivera: Great. On timing — we'd like to kick PoC early January. Budget wise, procurement asks for a basic T&Cs pack and pricing by Friday.
[07:55] Maya Chen: we'll aim to send pricing and security docs by end of week. Jordan will draft the PoC plan and dataset needs.
[08:03] Priya Patel: One more — how do you handle model versioning and rollbacks if a re-ranker regression happens?
[08:09] Jordan Lee: Console supports model pinning and rollouts, canarying, and performance regression alerts tied to evals. We also keep per-route stats so you can rollback quickly.
[08:22] Alex Rivera: Awesome. Thanks everyone.
[08:25] Maya Chen: Recap of next steps — we'll send pricing & security docs, Jordan will send PoC plan, Paladin to share samples and infra details — action items as noted. Thanks all.
[08:35] (call ends)

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-heard product names (e.g., "Redwood Deicated"), filler words present, occasional speaker label hiccups in the recording.
